findings.title: Three slice-level gates are configurable in v1, but only `pre-advance` has a state representation and cascade insertion point
findings.description: The `[workflow.review_gates]` table ("Config keys") defines three slice-level transitions — `pre-tasks`, `pre-implementation`, `pre-advance` — and "Initiative-level gating (v1 deferred)" states "V1 implements only the four slice-level transitions" (a miscount: the table holds three slice-level plus the initiative-level `pre-slice-plan`). But the two new `SliceStatus` values are defined exclusively at the tasks-complete position ("`pending-review` — tasks complete, review gate configured…", "`review-failed` — review artifact present, verdict does not clear the threshold"), and "Gate insertion point" designs exactly one new branch — "between current Priority 5 (`in-implementation`) and Priority 6 (`complete → advance`)" — returning `review`/`blocked` only for the advance case. Nothing in the document says where the `pre-tasks` gate fires in the `getNext()` cascade (between Priority 3 and 4?), what `SliceStatus` a slice holds while its design review is outstanding (the `pending-review` definition doesn't fit — tasks aren't complete), or what recommendation replaces `Create task breakdown (Phase 5)`. The same blind spot applies to `pre-implementation` and to the "ConsistencyChecker rule", which only checks the slice-plan-complete case. As written, the "First-class status representation" design goal is met for one of three v1 transitions, and the anticipated gate slice ("Add the new priority branch" — singular) would leave `pre-tasks`/`pre-implementation` config keys as dead configuration. Either narrow v1 to `pre-advance` explicitly or design the status/cascade treatment for the other two positions.

findings.title: Gate defaults are incomplete and self-contradictory: no default `reviewType`, and gate-activation semantics conflict
findings.description:
Two defects in the defaulting contract:

1. **No default `reviewType`.** The three global keys cover enablement (`review_enabled`), threshold (`review_threshold`), and unknown-verdict policy (`review_unknown_as`) — but the discovery rule matches "the current slice index and **configured reviewType**", and `reviewType` appears only inside per-gate overrides. With `review_enabled = true` and no `[workflow.review_gates]` section (the advertised "sensible defaults" path), the gate has no reviewType to match filenames against — it cannot look for anything. "When no per-transition override exists, `workflow.review_threshold` applies" supplies only the threshold, silently leaving the reviewType undefined.
2. **Contradictory activation semantics.** "Slice status extension" says "When `review_enabled = false` **or no gate is configured for the current transition**, the status goes directly from `complete` to advance", implying a transition needs a configured gate entry to be gated at all — directly contradicting the previous sentence that a missing override falls back to the global threshold (i.e., the gate still exists). An implementer cannot determine whether `review_enabled = true` alone gates `pre-advance`.

The promised fail-fast validation ("unrecognized per-gate config is a config error surfaced immediately", Architectural Principles) cannot be implemented against these undefined domains either.

findings.title: Verdict/threshold/policy vocabulary is inconsistent (`concerns` vs `concern` vs `CONCERNS`) and the value domains are never enumerated
findings.description: The threshold default is spelled `workflow.review_threshold = "concerns"` (plural), the verdict vocabulary is `CONCERNS` (uppercase), and Technical Considerations writes `workflow.review_unknown_as = "concern"` (singular) — three spellings of one concept across one document, in a design that promises strict validation of these exact strings. Worse, the domains are undefined: "`CONCERNS` — clears if `review_threshold = \"concerns\"` **or lower**" invokes an ordering whose lower values (below `concerns`, above the always-blocking `FAIL`) are never named; `review_unknown_as` shows `"fail"` and `"concern"` and the `pending-review` definition refers to "`review_unknown_as` treats it as pending" — a `"pending"` policy value defined nowhere in the config key comments or the verdict table. This directly violates the project rule "Never scatter comparison values across code. Define it once" — and the fail-fast `validate` hook cannot reject invalid values when the valid set is unstated.

findings.title: Decision matrix leaves UNKNOWN and read-failure status mapping ambiguous, contradicting the promised test matrix
findings.description: "Absent `verdict` field, unrecognized value, or file-read failure — treated as `UNKNOWN`, then `review_unknown_as` applies" — but the two slice statuses don't cover the outcome. `review-failed` is defined as "review artifact present, **verdict does not clear the threshold**", which misrepresents a file that could not be parsed (there is no verdict). `pending-review`'s parenthetical ("or verdict is `UNKNOWN` and `review_unknown_as` treats it as pending") covers only an undefined `"pending"` policy. So under the documented defaults (artifact exists, verdict unparseable, `review_unknown_as = "fail"`), the resulting status is unstated. The anticipated gate slice promises "Full unit test coverage against the verdict decision matrix and all `review_unknown_as` / `review_threshold` combinations" — but the matrix's rows for absent-verdict/unparseable-file are exactly the rows the architecture leaves undefined.

findings.title: Parse-failure rationale has no data path, and `deriveSliceStatus`'s blanket `catch` contradicts the stated failure behavior
findings.description: "File-read failure modes" states the failure "is treated as `UNKNOWN` and `review_unknown_as` applies. The rationale returned to the caller **names the parse failure explicitly**." Three gaps make this unbuildable as stated: (a) the parse site and verdict reader are never located — "Review-artifact discovery" only describes filename scanning, while `DocumentDetectionResult`'s sibling slots are bare paths (`string | null`); whether `documentDetector.ts` returns the path and `WorkflowNavigator` calls the existing `frontmatterParser.parseFrontmatter`, or the detector parses (mixing detection and parsing), is unspecified; (b) `SliceStatus` gains only two enum values and `NextAction` is frozen ("must not change the `NextAction` return type"), so there is no channel to carry the parse-failure detail from the parse site into the rationale built in `getNext()`; (c) `deriveSliceStatus()` (`packages/core/src/introspection/WorkflowNavigator.ts:446–497`) ends in `catch { return base; }` — any exception escaping the frontmatter read is swallowed into `no-active-slice`, silently bypassing the gate entirely. The design must state that read/parse errors are caught and converted to `UNKNOWN` inside the gate before the outer catch.

findings.title: Machine routing contract relies on user-facing `recommendation` strings while the document forbids the type change that would make it robust
findings.description: The gate returns `{ recommendation: "review", … }` / `{ recommendation: "blocked", … }` — machine-significant literals dropped into `NextAction.recommendation`, a free-string field whose existing values are human prose ("Continue implementation — 3 tasks remaining", "Advance to slice 241: …"). This is exactly the project rule "NEVER use user-accessible labels as logical structure": Amoeba/Squadron must string-match `"review"`/`"blocked"` to route to a review agent. The document simultaneously (a) claims in Design Goals that runners "can act on them **without parsing recommendation strings**", (b) states in Related Work that the runner "Depends on CF returning **structured** `recommendation` values with a stable vocabulary", and (c) forbids changing `NextAction` ("must not change the `NextAction` return type") — which forecloses adding an optional structured field (e.g. `gateState: 'pending-review' | 'review-failed'`) that would resolve the contradiction. As written, either the Design Goal is false or the runner contract is label-matching. Note also the terminology drift: the Overview says the gate "returns a `pending-review` or `review-failed` recommendation" while the actual `recommendation` values are `"review"`/`"blocked"` — consumers reading the Overview will match the wrong strings.

findings.title: Discovery pattern is stricter than the established naming convention and the reviewType source is ambiguous — valid reviews can be silently invisible
findings.description: The rule matches `NNN-review.{reviewType}.*.md`, requiring a reviewType **filename segment** and a non-empty trailing name segment. But the existing conventions this document claims to reuse don't work that way: `packages/core/src/schema/frontmatterSchema.ts` parses review filenames as `NNN-review.{free-form-name}.md` (`FILENAME_PARTS_RE = /^(\d+)-(…|review|…)\.(.+?)(?:-\d+)?\.md$/i` — everything after `review.` is one opaque name), and slice 905 treats `reviewType` as a **frontmatter** field ("if docType is review, reviewType must be present"). Consequences: a review named `210-review.github-copilot-comparison.md` (valid per the existing convention, no type segment) matches the gate's pattern never — the artifact-first gate then reports `pending-review` despite a review existing, a silent wrong verdict in the blocking direction. Likewise `210-review.code.md` (type but no trailing segment) fails the glob. The claim "The existing naming convention … is the pattern — no new convention is introduced" is unverifiable in this checkout (`project-documents/user/reviews/` and `file-naming-conventions.md` are absent; the only corroborating example, `301-review.slice.judge-enforcement-layer.md` in `001-review-gating-architecture-input.context-forge.md`, is consistent with the pattern but not proof of it). The design must state whether reviewType is filename-derived or frontmatter-derived, and per the project's lenient-parsing rule, match `NNN-review.*.md` and filter on frontmatter `reviewType` (or fall back explicitly) rather than silently missing files.

findings.title: Multi-match tie-break: "lexicographically last filename (most recent by sort order)" is a false claim and can select a stale verdict
findings.description: Filename suffixes are semantic names (e.g. `github-copilot-vs-code-ide-support`), not timestamps — lexicographic order does not track recency. With `210-review.code.aaa-copilot.md` (new, PASS) and `210-review.code.zzz-march-audit.md` (old, FAIL), the rule deterministically picks the stale FAIL and blocks the advance. "Deterministic and documented" is true but insufficient: the gate silently resolves conflicting verdicts by an ordering that has no relationship to which review is current. Use `dateUpdated` frontmatter or mtime for recency, or — per "Never use silent fallback values" — fail explicitly with a `review-conflict` condition when multiple matching reviews disagree.

findings.title: Review frontmatter schema has two claimed owners: Squadron slice 300 contract vs. CF's existing `FRONTMATTER_SCHEMAS.review`
findings.description: "The review artifact's frontmatter schema (`verdict`, `score`, `criteria`, `provenance`) is owned by Squadron slice 300. CF reads it but does not define it. … CF must not extend or reinterpret this schema unilaterally." But CF already defines and enforces a review frontmatter schema: `packages/core/src/schema/frontmatterSchema.ts` (source of truth "derived from file-naming-conventions.md") declares `FRONTMATTER_SCHEMAS.review` requiring `docType`, `project`, `status`, `dateCreated`, `dateUpdated`, and `ConsistencyChecker` Rule 12 validates it. The principle as written makes CF's own existing schema a unilateral violation. The contract statement must be scoped: the Squadron-owned subset is `verdict`/`score`/`criteria`/`provenance`; the document envelope remains CF's. Relatedly, "It carries `criteria` and `provenance` as opaque fields … they are preserved for downstream tools that do consume them" describes work with no defined surface — CF never rewrites review artifacts, and no `SliceStatus`/`NextAction`/result type is designated to carry these fields.

findings.title: `review` slot type, score storage, and the "stateless" navigator are mutually unresolved
findings.description: "`DocumentDetectionResult` gains a `review` slot" never states the type. The sibling slots are paths (`sliceDesign: string | null`, `taskFile: string[] | null`), but the gate needs `verdict` — and "Score-based gating … is read and **stored** when present" invokes a store that doesn't exist: `WorkflowNavigator` is documented as a "Stateless workflow navigator", `NextAction` is frozen, and the `SliceStatus` extension adds only enum values, no fields. If "stored" means "surfaced", the surface is missing; if it means persisted, state ownership is undefined. Define the slot (path-only, parsed via the existing `frontmatterParser`, or a small `{ path, verdict, score }` shape), place verdict parsing in one component, and either drop "stored" or name the store.

findings.title: Priority renumbering is assigned to two different slices, and the stated rationale is contradicted by existing code
findings.description: "Anticipated Slices" puts "renumbering the `getNext()` priority cascade" in slice 1 (which explicitly has "No gate logic yet"), while Technical Considerations says "The slice implementing the gate logic should renumber the full cascade … as part of the same change" — the same work assigned to two slices. Additionally, "requires renumbering to avoid fractional priorities" is moot: `getNext()` already uses fractional labels (`// Priority 2.5` at `WorkflowNavigator.ts:187`). Converting to named stages in whichever slice touches the cascade resolves both.

findings.title: "No 160 interfaces change" is inaccurate
findings.description: `DocumentDetectionResult`, `SliceStatus`, and the `NextAction.recommendation` vocabulary are all 160-era interfaces being extended by this work; even if additive, construction sites break — e.g. the `detectDocuments` mock in `packages/core/tests/introspection/ConsistencyChecker.test.ts:93` must gain the new `review` field. "No 160 interfaces break; additions only" would be accurate.
